message.content:
**Typical time difference**

| City | Standard Time | Daylight‑Saving Time | UTC offset | Typical difference |
|------|---------------|----------------------|------------|--------------------|
| Los Angeles (Pacific) | PST | PDT | UTC‑8 / UTC‑7 | **9 hours** (Berlin ahead) |
| Berlin (Central Europe) | CET | CEST | UTC+1 / UTC+2 | **9 hours** (Berlin ahead) |

So for most of the year, Berlin is **9 hours ahead** of Los Angeles.

---

**When the difference is 8 hours**

Because the start and end dates for daylight‑saving time (DST) don’t line up exactly, there are short windows each year when the two cities are on different DST schedules:

| Period | Los Angeles | Berlin | UTC offset | Difference |
|--------|-------------|--------|------------|------------|
| **Early spring** | PDT (UTC‑7) | CET (UTC+1) | 8 hours |
| **Late fall** | PST (UTC‑8) | CEST (UTC+2) | 8 hours |

- **Spring transition** – Los Angeles switches to DST on the second Sunday in March, while Berlin switches on the last Sunday in March.  
  *Example (2024):* From March 10 to March 25, Los Angeles is UTC‑7 and Berlin is UTC+1 → 8 hours difference.

- **Fall transition** – Berlin ends DST on the last Sunday in October, Los Angeles on the first Sunday in November.  
  *Example (2024):* From October 27 to November 3, Los Angeles is UTC‑7 and Berlin is UTC+1 → 8 hours difference.

Outside those windows, the difference reverts to 9 hours.

---

### Quick reference

| Date range (2024) | Difference |
|-------------------|------------|
| Jan 1 – Mar 9     | 9 h |
| Mar 10 – Mar 25   | 8 h |
| Mar 26 – Oct 26   | 9 h |
| Oct 27 – Nov 3    | 8 h |
| Nov 4 – Dec 31    | 9 h |

*(Adjust dates each year based on the DST rules.)*

So, unless you’re looking at those brief transition periods, just add 9 hours to Los Angeles time to get Berlin time.
